instructions: Rinse the 1 cup millet in a fine-mesh strainer under running water, then drain it.
Put 6 cups of water in a large pot over high heat and bring it to a boil.
Meanwhile, heat a dry skillet over medium-high heat and add the millet. Stir it often for 5 to 8 minutes, until it smells toasty. Millet burns easily, so don't walk away.
Carefully add the toasted millet to the boiling water and stir. When it comes back to a boil, turn the heat down to low.
Simmer, uncovered, for 20 minutes, stirring now and then so nothing sticks to the bottom. The water will turn golden and a little starchy, and the millet won't soak up all of it.
Stir in the 1/2 tsp salt. If you'd like it thicker, simmer it for a few minutes longer.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Serve in bowls, stirring 1/2 tbsp of the sugar into each of the 4 bowls.
To keep it, cool the porridge, cover it and refrigerate it for up to 4 days. It thickens as it sits, so stir in a splash of water when you reheat it in a pot over medium-low heat or in the microwave.
method_notes: Mayuri's Jikoni, Food.com and Seduce Your Tastebuds all rinse the millet and simmer it in plenty of water, then serve it plain or with a little sweetener. None of them showed a real rating (Food.com has one review), so the lead is Food.com, the only version with a toasting step and a full ratio. Water runs from about 3.5 cups per cup of millet (Food.com) to 8 to 12 cups (Mayuri's thin congee); this uses 6 for a porridge you can spoon. Wuxi-style versions with adzuki beans and peanuts were left out to keep it nut-free. Sugar is served on the side so it stays vegan. The fridge time is a general guideline for cooked grains.
